lesson.title: Beauty, Combat, and a Trade-Off with Survival: Sexual Selection
lesson.summary: Sexual selection is a special mode of natural selection based specifically on success at mating rather than survival, and it can favor traits, like a peacock's tail, that would otherwise look like liabilities under ordinary survival based selection.
lesson.body:
Recall that natural selection acts on relative fitness: differences in how many surviving, reproducing offspring different genotypes leave behind, not differences in survival alone. Sexual selection narrows that idea to one specific component of fitness, success at obtaining mates. It was Darwin's own answer to a puzzle his broader theory of natural selection could not easily explain. Some traits, most famously the peacock's enormous, brightly colored tail, are costly to grow, make an animal slower, and make it more visible to predators, so by ordinary survival logic they should have been eliminated by selection long ago. Sexual selection resolves the puzzle by recognizing that survival is not the only thing fitness depends on. An individual that survives but never mates leaves no offspring at all, so a trait that boosts mating success can be favored by selection even if it comes at some cost to survival.

Sexual selection operates through two related mechanisms. Intrasexual selection is competition between members of the same sex, usually males, for access to mates, favoring traits like large body size, weapons such as antlers or horns, or aggressive behavior that help an individual win direct contests with rivals. Intersexual selection is mate choice: one sex, often females, choosing to mate preferentially with partners that display particular traits, favoring whatever phenotype those choosers find appealing, generation after generation. The peacock's tail is the classic example of the second kind. Peahens that choose to mate with males bearing longer, more elaborate tails leave more offspring carrying the genotype for that same elaborate tail, and as those offspring's phenotypes are shaped by that genotype the way their fathers' were, the trait becomes more common and more exaggerated over generations, even as it makes males somewhat easier for predators to catch.

The reason sexual selection deserves its own name, rather than being folded into ordinary natural selection, is this built in tension: a trait under strong sexual selection can be actively opposed by ordinary survival based selection at the very same time. The peacock's tail is a net benefit to relative fitness only because the reproductive advantage it provides outweighs its survival cost. If predation pressure rose high enough, or if peahens' preferences shifted, that balance could tip the other way. This is a useful reminder of how broad relative fitness really is: it is always about total reproductive output across a lifetime, survival and mating success combined, not about which individual is fastest, biggest, or best camouflaged. Sexual selection is simply what happens when the mating half of that equation pulls hard enough in its own direction to shape a trait almost independently of the survival half.
